context:
Goal: the check catches the copies that actually happened.
Problem (rule): the real incident copies were 5-word fragments. An 8-word floor misses all of them.
Based on (test): measured on main 5a5f081e: nine files hold a 5-word run of the old sentence, none an 8-word run.
Departs from: main has no reword check — adds one that counts runs of 5 words or more.

lastAnswer.note: i dont really understand this question

options.gain: Catches the incident that started this.
options.label: Yes: 5 words (recommended)
options.lose: More false alarms on short stock phrases; the rate on other sentences is unmeasured.

options.label: No: 8 words
options.lose: Misses the copies that actually happened.

reply: You picked a. Plainly: when a rule's wording changes, old copies of the old wording can stay behind in other files. The check looks for leftover runs of the old words. The question was how many words in a row must match before the check calls it a copy. The real copies that started this were only 5 words long, so a 5-word bar catches them, and an 8-word bar would miss them all. The cost of 5 is that a common short phrase may sometimes trip it. Home: step one-home-check. Closed 12:40 CST.
